rows.speaker: cumhûr
rows.claim: Most commentators, following Abu Hayyan, take Iram as a major city belonging to Aad, also called Zat al-Imad.
rows.anchor: cumhûrun kavlince burada “İrem” Âd’e mensub olan bir medine, yani büyük bir şehir ismidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported legend says Shaddad ibn Aad built an earthly imitation of Paradise over many years, but he and his family died before entering it.
rows.anchor: Şeddâd b. Âd tarafından ona nazîr olmak üzere yeryüzünde âdeten bulunması muhal veya müsteb‘ad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı treats the Garden of Iram story as an imaginative parable of those who deny the afterlife yet seek Paradise in this world and are deprived.
rows.anchor: Şeddâd’ın cenneti Bâğ-ı İrem muhayyel bir efsanedir. Âhireti inkar edip de dünyada iken cennete girmek isteyenlerin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that a Muslim would enter Iram and that Abdullah ibn Kilaba found it while searching for his camel are unsound; Ibn Hajar called the report fabricated.
rows.anchor: Abdullah b. Kılâbe’nin devesini ararken ona girdiğine dair bir rivayet naklederlerse de sahih değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka‘b identified the city as Alexandria, while Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Maqburi identified it with Damascus; critics instead place Aad in the Ahqaf between Oman and Hadramawt.
rows.anchor: İbn Müseyyeb ve Makbürî[^37] Dımaşk demişler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı suggests those locations may reflect a view that the later Aad, perhaps the Amalekites, once occupied Alexandria and Syria; the city interpretation refers to this later Aad.
rows.anchor: belki bir vakitler İskenderiye ve Şam taraflarını da istîlâ etmiş olan Amâlika’nın

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many place Iram in Yemen, and Marib is a plausible identification.
rows.anchor: Çokları İrem şehrinin Yemen’de olduğuna kāildirler ki bunun Me’rib olması da pek melhuzdur

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: Reading Aad as two peoples, al-Kashshaf identifies Aad al-Ula with Hud’s people and Aad al-Ukhra with Iram.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf Âd-ı Ûlâ kavm-i Hûd, Âd-ı Uhrâ İrem diye zikretmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the city reading, Iram is construed as an explanatory apposition to Aad with “people of Iram” understood, or as a partitive apposition; Zat al-Imad is its adjective or apposition.
rows.anchor: “İrem” Âd’dan atf-ı beyan olmak için “ehl-i İrem” takdîrinde olmak veya bedel-i iştimal yapılmak iktizâ eyler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three grammatical readings can describe the tent-dwelling first Aad, the city-dwelling later Aad, or both Aad peoples together.
rows.anchor: Birinci vecihte ashâb-ı hayme olan Âd-ı Ûlâ’nın vasfı, üçüncü vecihte ise ikisine de muhtemil

none: Turkish translation of the verses only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may narrow provision as a test that earns afterlife reward according to a person’s patience; its light worldly burden and great reward are themselves care.
rows.anchor: Rabbi onu imtihan eder sabrına göre âhirette mükâfat etmek üzere imtihan muamelesi yapar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mistaken person reads scarcity as contempt, overlooks other divine gifts, and values worldly pleasure over virtue; even little provision deserves gratitude.
rows.anchor: Rızık az da olsa yine şükrü bilinmek lâzım geldiğini ve azın kadrini bilmeyen çoğunkini de bilmeyeceğini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither abundance nor scarcity by itself proves honor or humiliation; both are tests whose outcome depends on success in the trial.
rows.anchor: İkisi de birer imtihandır. Hüküm, imtihanda muvaffakiyete

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What seems like honor may end in humiliation as a deceptive reprieve, while apparent disgrace may prove protective and end in honor.
rows.anchor: ikram sanılan bir istidrac ile neticede zillet, ihânet sanılan da bir vikāye ile neticede ikram çıkacaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke advances from words to deeds and from an individual to the collective, sharpening the admonition and directing people toward noble conduct.
rows.anchor: Kavlî takbihten fiilî takbîhe, ferdden cem‘e intikal ile tekdir ve tevbihte terakki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those demanding honor from God fail their own duty when they do not treat orphans generously with the resources God gave them.
rows.anchor: Doğrusu siz vazifelerinizi yapmazken Rabbinizden ne yüzle ikram beklersiniz ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should compete in urging one another to feed and care for the poor, but instead they discourage it and may seek to exploit them.
rows.anchor: birbirinizle müsabaka etmeniz lâzım gelirken siz bilakis ondan kaçınıyor, birbirinizi tenfir ediyorsunuz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal verb is originally tatāhāddūn; Nafi, Ibn Kathir, and Ibn Amir read it with a damma on ha and without the alif.
rows.anchor: Nâfi‘, İbn Kesîr, İbn Âmir kıraatlerinde hâ’nın zammıyla elifsiz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Amr and Yaqub read the verbs throughout in the third-person plural: they honor, urge, consume, and love.
rows.anchor: Ebû Amr ve Ya‘kūb kıraatlerinde de bu fiiller hep yâ ile gāib sîgası üzerine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turath derives from warath, meaning inheritance; its initial waw changes to ta because it is vowelled with damma.
rows.anchor: “Türâs” aslı وراث olup miras demektir. Vâv mazmum olmakla tâ’ya kalbolunmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lemm can mean gathering without distinction or settling somewhere; describing eating here, it suggests indiscriminate, greedy consumption or taking inherited wealth without asking its source.
rows.anchor: “Lemm” iyisine kötüsüne bakmayıp cem‘etmek, derip toplamak, bir de bir yere inip konmak mânalarına gelir

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Exegetes censure heirs who greedily seize the inheritance without respecting orphans’ and other heirs’ rights, or squander unearned inheritances in luxury.
rows.anchor: Müfessirînin beyânına göre murad, yetimlerin ve vereseden sâirlerinin hukūkunu gözetmeyerek hırs ile mirasın hepsine konmak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People love wealth intensely and pile it up, forgetting that spendthrift heirs may waste what the hoarder failed to spend for good, leaving the owner only sin.
rows.anchor: Öyle bir seviş ki {جَمًّۭا} çok, yığmacasına

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These failures come from neglecting the afterlife and God’s watch; people should use their present opportunity for good, honor orphans, feed the poor, and prepare for the hereafter.
rows.anchor: Bütün bunlar âhireti düşünmemek, Hak teâlâ’nın mirsâd ile gözetmekte olduğunu hesâba almamaktan neş’et eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s crushing recalls the description in al-Haqqa of earth and mountains being reduced in one blow.
rows.anchor: Sûre-i Hâkka’da وَحُمِلَتِ ٱلْأَرْضُ وَٱلْجِبَالُ فَدُكَّتَا دَكَّةًۭ وَٰحِدَةًۭ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated dakk means successive, comprehensive crushing, like saying people arrived in wave after wave, rather than mere emphasis.
rows.anchor: Bu tekrar mücerred tekid için değil istî‘âb ve tevâlîyi ifade içindir

rows.speaker: Münzir b. Saîd
rows.claim: God’s coming means manifestation to creation, not movement from place to place; the same idiom applies to the coming of the Calamity and the Deafening Blast.
rows.anchor: Münzir b. Saîd demiştir ki: “Bu mecî’in mânası nukle mecî’i

rows.speaker: bir kısım müfessirîn
rows.claim: Some exegetes understand the phrase through an omitted noun: the Lord’s command, judgment, decree, or overpowering arrives.
rows.anchor: hazf-i muzâf ile وَجَاءَ اَمْرُ رَبِّكَ Rabbinin emri, hükm ü kazâsı veya kahrı geldiği vakit demektir

rows.speaker: birçok müfessirîn
rows.claim: Many take it as an image of the appearance of God’s signs of power and sovereignty, like a ruler personally appearing amid his ministers and troops.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ’nın kudret ve saltanatı âyâtının zuhur ve tebeyyününü temsil olduğuna kāil olmuşlardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is brought into view and exposed to the misguided so clearly that they can no longer deny or avoid it, as stated in al-Shu‘ara.
rows.anchor: azgınlar için ibraz ve izhar olunmuş, artık inkârına, ihtirâzına imkân kalmayacak surette meydana çıkarılmıştır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second “that day” substitutes for the preceding “when”; on that day the heedless person finally understands truths ignored in life, but too late to act.
rows.anchor: o insan anlar o gāfil insan evvel dünyada anlamadığı hakikati o gün anlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Late understanding can only make the person feel punishment, loss, longing, and regret, because the chance to return and act has passed.
rows.anchor: iş işten geçmiş, geri dönüp de bir iş yapmak ihtimâli kalmamış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Presenting good deeds beforehand means preparing righteous works; the lām in “for my life” can mean purpose, referring to the afterlife, or time, referring to worldly life.
rows.anchor: Takdimden murad ilerisi için önceden hayırlı ameller yapmaktır. لِحَيَاتِى’de lâm ta‘lîl ve tevkīt içindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the pronouns refer to God, no one can punish or bind as severely as God, describing the severity of that day’s punishment.
rows.anchor: Birisi Allah’a râci‘olmasıdır ki “Allah’ın o gün o insana ettiği azâbı kimse edemez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı prefers taking the pronouns as referring to the human: the sinner inflicts this punishment on himself through disbelief and evil deeds, as in al-Nisa.
rows.anchor: Birisi de insana râci‘olmasıdır ki bu daha râcihtir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the passive readings of al-Kisa’i and Yaqub, the pronoun must refer to the person: no one is tortured or bound like that person.
rows.anchor: Kisâî ve Ya‘kūb kıraatlerinde لَّا يُعَذِّبُ ve ذال, وَلَا يُوثِقُ’in ve ثا’nın fethiyle mechul okunur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passage contrasts the fate of the person attached to worldly pleasures with that of the soul content with God, His remembrance, obedience, and approval.
rows.anchor: Dünyaya gönül bağlayan ve itmi’nânını ancak dünya lezâizinde bulan kâfir insanın âkıbeti bu olduğu anlatıldıktan sonra

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father and what he begets are additional objects of the oath, coordinated with the sacred city; the terms mean a father and his offspring.
rows.anchor: Evvelki هٰذَا الْبَلَدِ üzerine ma‘tuf olarak bunlar da muksemun bihtir: “Vâlid” ata, “mâ-veled”

rows.speaker: Mücâhid
rows.claim: “The father” is Adam and “what he begets” is his descendants; humanity merits the oath for its remarkable gifts and role in knowledge, prophecy, and religion.
rows.anchor: Mücâhid’den mervîdir.[^1] Bunlara kasem edilmesi

rows.speaker: bir kısım müfessirîn
rows.claim: A narrower interpretation takes the oath as Adam and his righteous descendants, since the unrighteous are likened to livestock and described as deaf, dumb, and blind.
rows.anchor: bir de denilmiştir ki kasem, Âdem ile evlâdından sâlihînedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies the father as Abraham and the offspring as Ishmael and Muhammad, or Abraham and Ishmael with Muhammad as the offspring, linking the oath to Mecca.
rows.anchor: “Vâlid” İbrâhim ve “mâ-veled” İsmâil ve Muhammed aleyhimüsselâm, yahut

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Abrahamic reading, “ma” can also signal wonder at an extraordinary child, as in the wording of 3:36 and the oath in 91:5.
rows.anchor: “ma”nın bir taaccüb mânasına da îmâ etmesidir ki, “acîbü’ş-şân mevlud” demek olur

rows.speaker: Ebû İmran
rows.claim: A report from Abu Imran says the father is Abraham and the offspring are all his children; Elmalılı says this must be restricted to believers because 2:124 excludes wrongdoers from God’s covenant.
rows.anchor: İbn Cerîr ve İbn Ebî Hâtim, Ebû İmran’dan: “Vâlid” İbrâhim aleyhisselâm ve “mâ-veled” onun cemî‘-i veledi

rows.speaker: Mâverdî
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi also allows that the father is the Prophet and his offspring are his community.
rows.anchor: Maverdî’den: “Vâlid” Hazret-i Peygamber sallallâhu aleyhi ve sellem ve “mâ-veled” ümmeti olmak

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to interpret the wording as every father and child; al-Tabari calls this correct, and al-Razi says it fittingly includes the sanctity of all people and living creatures born.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’a nisbet olunarak denilmiştir ki: Murad, her vâlid ve mevluddur

rows.speaker: İkrime tarikiyle İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Another report says “the father” means every one who gives birth and “what does not give birth” the non-birthing; this may be a relative clause or a negation embracing all things.
rows.anchor: İkrime tarîkiyle yine İbn Abbas’tan bir de şu rivayet edilmiştir ki: “‘Vâlid’ her bir doğuran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “ma” is negative, the construction needs an omitted relative that Basran grammarians do not permit, so that interpretation is weak.
rows.anchor: Basriyyûn tecviz etmemiş olduklarından bu vecih zayıf addedilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan context favors Abraham and Ishmael; taken generally, the most apparent sense is every father and child, which also includes the earlier interpretations.
rows.anchor: Atfa nazaran en zâhiri bu beldeye münasebeti mâruf olan vâlid ve veled olmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority’s sense of kabad is that humanity was created amid hardship: life develops through severe trials, by divine care, so people should endure, give thanks, and show mercy to sufferers.
rows.anchor: mihnet ve meşakkat içinden insanlık gayesine ermek insan hilkatinin bir lâzımı ve Hâlık’ın bir kanunudur

rows.speaker: Sâhib-Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf derives kabad from liver pain or swelling, then its sense broadens to toil and hardship; mukabada, struggling against hardship, comes from it.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf der ki: “‘Kebed’, aslı كَبِدَ الرَّجُلُ كَبَدًا فـَهُوَ أَكْبَدُ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others make severity the basic meaning, citing the thickening or solidifying of milk; this reverses the first account’s derivation from the organ to hardship.
rows.anchor: Bu iki kavil arasında fark evvelkisinde “kebed” ismi ciğere mevzû‘yapılmış

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: Another view takes kabad as uprightness or steadiness, perhaps from the straight liver or the expression “kabad of heaven”; it sees humans standing upright and spiritually capable of ascent.
rows.anchor: “Kebed”, istivâ ve istikāmet mânasına denilmiştir ki ciğerin düzgünlüğünden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı considers deriving the uprightness sense from the vowelled form kabad a very remote interpretation.
rows.anchor: feth ile “kebed”den bu mânaya intikal çok ba‘îddir

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: A third view reads kabad as the strength of human constitution, with God giving the body strength; this can be included within the hardship sense.
rows.anchor: “Kebed” hilkatin şiddet ve kuvveti denilmiştir

rows.speaker: Keşfü’l-Esrâr
rows.claim: Kashf al-Asrar offers a physiological analogy of bodily membranes, vessels, and circulation to illustrate how life and formation emerge through stages of condensation.
rows.anchor: Bu bize bazı zamanlar nutfenin tehassür ve incimâdında husûle gelen hâli anlatabilir

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: On the hardship reading, Razi says the verse can encompass worldly, religious, and afterlife trials, or all of them together; the comprehensive reading is correct.
rows.anchor: Birinci veche göre murad yalnız dünya şedâidi olmak da, yalnız tekâlîf şedâidi olmak da

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Worldly hardship covers each stage from passage through the loins and womb, nursing and puberty, earning a livelihood, and finally death.
rows.anchor: Sulbden geçerken ve anasının karnında, sonra emzik zamanında, sonra bulûğunda

rows.speaker: Hasan
rows.claim: Religious hardship means giving thanks in joy, remaining patient in distress, and laboring to fulfill acts of worship.
rows.anchor: Hasan demiştir ki: ‘Meserret hâlinde şükür ile uğraşır, sıkıntı hâlinde sabır ile uğraşır

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Afterlife hardship proceeds through death, questioning by angels, the grave, resurrection, and standing before God until one reaches Paradise or Hell.
rows.anchor: Âhiret şedâidi, ölüm, melek suâli, kabir zulmeti, sonra ba‘s ve Allah’a arz

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Razi adds that worldly pleasures are only relief from pain: food relieves hunger and clothes relieve heat or cold, so life alternates between pain and respite.
rows.anchor: Bu dünyada lezzet yoktur, o lezzet zannedilenler elemden

rows.speaker: Râzî
rows.claim: Because a wise Creator would not make pain the ultimate purpose, and nonexistence would equally avoid pleasure and pain, human hardship implies a necessary afterlife of happiness and honor.
rows.anchor: bu dünya yurdundan başka bir âhiret yurdu lâzımdır ki orası saadet, lezzet, keramet yurdu olsun

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: A second interpretation takes kabad as uprightness: unlike animals that move head-down, humans stand erect, which is a blessing in their creation.
rows.anchor: ‘fî kebed: diğer hayvânât menkûsen baş aşağı yürürlerken insan yukarı doğru kāim

rows.speaker: Kelbî
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse was revealed about Abu al-Ashadd of Banu Jumah, whose strength was said to keep him immovable even when leather was pulled from beneath his feet.
rows.anchor: Kelbî demiştir ki ‘bu âyet Benî Cumah’tan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a particular occasion of revelation is possible, “human” means humanity in general, not a single named person; the hardship interpretation is the intended one.
rows.anchor: Sebeb-i nüzul hâs olabilirse de “insan”dan murad bazılarının sandığı gibi muayyen bir insan değil, âmmdır

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Al-Alusi regards all interpretations besides hardship and toil as weak; he reports that al-Hakim authenticated the hardship report from Ibn Abbas and others transmitted it from early authorities.
rows.anchor: Kebed hakkında birinci mihnet ve meşakkat mânasından mâ‘adâ akvâlin hepsi zayıftır, itimad edilmez

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse first consoles and encourages the Prophet by stating that hardship is built into human life, then rebukes arrogant opponents who disrespect him; the earlier promise of success is recalled.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah’a bir tesliye ve teşvik yapıldıktan ve daha önceden وَأَنتَ حِلٌّۢ بِهَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدِ vaadiyle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the question refers to humanity generally but specifically targets proud, arrogant people; the question is a rebuke, though astonishment is also proposed.
rows.anchor: İstifham tevbih içindir, taaccüb için de denilmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The occasion has been associated with several boastful opponents: Abu al-Ashadd, Amr ibn Abd Wadd, Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, and al-Harith ibn Amir.
rows.anchor: Amr b. Abdi Ved denilmiş, Velid b. Mugīre denilmiş, Ebû Cehil b. Hişam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boast about heaps of wealth was made to flaunt superiority before believers; calling the spending waste signals that it brought no genuine benefit, unlike feeding the poor.
rows.anchor: Bunu mü’minlere karşı azamet satmak üzere gurur ve iftihar ile söylüyor ve gösteriş için sarfettiği malları kasdediyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the wealth was spent in hostility toward the Messenger, to display the intensity of enmity.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah’a adâvetinin şiddetini izhar için ona düşmanlık yolunda sarfettiği malları kasdettiği de söylenmiştir

rows.speaker: Mukātil
rows.claim: Al-Harith ibn Nawfal reportedly complained that since obeying Muhammad he had spent much on expiations and liabilities; this was resentment toward religion and refusal to obey the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Mukātil’den mervîdir ki: Hâris b. Nevfel bir günah işlediği zaman Resûlullah’tan istiftâ ederdi

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: Some read “he says” as future: the boast will be made at the Resurrection when the speaker discovers that his spending did not benefit him.
rows.anchor: يَقُولُ hâl değil, istikbal içindir. Bunu kıyamet günü söyleyecek demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad means a great quantity piled layer upon layer, like felt.
rows.anchor: “Lübed” “sured” vezninde çok mal mânasınadır ki, sanki birbiri üstüne yığıla yığıla keçe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question warns that God saw the spendthrift’s acts, will punish him for wasteful display or enmity, and he will regret it.
rows.anchor: Şüphe yok ki sarf ve ihlâk ettiyse onu Ehad olan Allah teâlâ görmüştür

rows.speaker: Kelbî
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi also reads the question as exposing a lie: the man claims to have spent much but spent nothing, and God knows what he truly did.
rows.anchor: Kelbî’den rivayet edildiği üzere sarf iddiasını tekzibdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elmalılı prefers the warning interpretation because it can also imply that the boast was false.
rows.anchor: Evvelki vecih, bu mânayı da işrab edebileceği için daha müfiddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s gifts guide humanity toward its purpose and establish divine knowledge and power to reckon and punish; the contrast between tranquil and unbelieving souls further explains hardship.
rows.anchor: halkettiği insana ve bu meyanda bilhassa kuvvet ve malıyla iftihar eden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The steep ascent is a difficult, elevated undertaking whose conquest calls for great courage.
rows.anchor: o akabe, iktihâmı büyük bir kahramanlık olan o zor yüksek iş, o sarp yokuş nedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Neck” is a part-for-whole metaphor for a person, especially a slave; releasing a neck means freeing an enslaved person, with freeing a slave as the simplest example.
rows.anchor: “rakabe” boyun demek olup zikr-i cüz irâde-i kül tarîkiyle mecaz olarak zat ve şahıs mânasında müte‘âreftir

rows.speaker: Ebû Hüreyre
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says whoever frees a believing slave has each of his own limbs freed from Hell in return for the corresponding limb, down to the private parts; it is transmitted in major hadith collections.
rows.anchor: Buhârî, Müslim, Tirmizî ve sâirede Ebû Hüreyre radıyallahu anh’tan mervîdir

rows.speaker: Berâ’
rows.claim: A Bedouin asked for a deed leading to Paradise; the Prophet distinguished freeing a person by oneself from helping to manumit a slave, saying the latter is broader and may be shared.
rows.anchor: İmam Ahmed ve İbn Hibban ve İbn Merdûye ve Beyhakī, Berâ’ radıyallahu anh’tan rivayet eylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If freeing one person is such a virtue, freeing an entire people or community is an even greater act of courage.
rows.anchor: Bir ferdi hürriyete kavuşturmak böyle büyük bir fazilet ve kahramanlık olunca bir kavmin, bir cemaatin hürriyetini kurtarmak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second meaning is rescuing oneself from Hell through righteous deeds, since each person is held by what he has earned; this requires struggle against the commanding soul and Satan.
rows.anchor: her nefsin halâsı kazancına bağlı olduğu için insanın a‘mâl-i sâliha kesbiyle kendisini cehennem azâbından kurtarması demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The failure of the proud person to overcome the ascent reflects his failure to struggle against his lower desires and Satan’s temptations.
rows.anchor: nefs-i emmârenin azgın hevâlarıyla Şeytan’ın iğvâlarına karşı mücahede etmekle olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mesghaba is a verbal noun for hunger, especially hunger amid hardship and fatigue; Abu Hayyan says it can also refer to thirst.
rows.anchor: “Mesğabe” “seğab”dan mimli masdar ki açlık ve bâhusus meşakkat ve yorgunluk içinde açlık

rows.speaker: Ebû Hayyân
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says mesghaba means widespread famine; its generality follows from dhi, which describes a day characterized by hunger, rather than merely a day of hunger.
rows.anchor: Ebû Hayyân’ın beyânına göre umûmî olan açlıktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding people during a widespread famine can save lives and is therefore a major act of courage like freeing a slave.
rows.anchor: Fi’l-vâki‘böyle umûmî bir açlık zamanında yemek yedirebilmek can kurtarmak demek olduğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphan is described as having kinship; this most naturally means blood relation, though neighborly closeness is possible, and lineage and religious ties are especially weighty.
rows.anchor: Karâbeti olan, yani yakınlığı olan bir yetime ki zâhiri, neseb yakınlığıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A miskin “with dust” is one in extreme poverty; the Turkish idiom of bedding on the ground and leaning on a stone conveys desperate need.
rows.anchor: “Zâ metrabe” Türkçemizde “toprak döşenip taş yaslanan” tâbir edildiği vechile şiddetli fakr u ihtiyaçtan kinayedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding a near orphan or destitute person during general famine requires heart and effort; the boastful person with abundant wealth did not undertake this ascent.
rows.anchor: bu akabeyi iktiham edemedi, böyle bir kahramanlığa hiçbir vechile girişemediği gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because “then he was” is coordinated with “he undertook,” the sense is negative: he neither attempted the ascent nor became one of the believers.
rows.anchor: Bu اقْتَحَمَ,كَانَ üzerine ma‘tuf olduğundan mâna menfîdir; فَلاَ اقـْتَحَمَ وَلاَ كَانَ demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers also encourage one another to patience and mercy, giving consolation and strength even when they cannot perform the demanding acts of freeing and feeding.
rows.anchor: iman edip de birbirlerine sabır tavsiye eden, merhamet tavsiye eyleyen sabırlı, merhametli mü’minlerden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of the right are blessed to themselves and others and receive their records on the right.
rows.anchor: kitapları sağ taraflarından verilecek ashâb-ı yemin, kendilerine ve başkalarına uğurlu kimselerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who disbelieve in God’s signs, including the arrogant man, are people of ill omen whose records are given on the left and who bring harm to themselves and others.
rows.anchor: Onlar şeâmet sâhipleridir. Meş’umluktan kurtulmayan, kitapları sollarından verilecek ashâb-ı şimâl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mu’sada is the passive participle of isad, to shut or lock tightly; sealing the fire over them conveys the severity and everlasting nature of punishment.
rows.anchor: “Mu’sade” “îsâd”dan ism-i mef‘uldür. آصَدْتُ الْبَابَ denir ki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duha literally describes the sun rising above the visible horizon and its light spreading; by extension it names the morning period, with dahwa, duha, and daha marking successively later hours.
rows.anchor: “duhâ”nın asıl hakikati Güneş’in doğduğu mer’î ufuktan yükselip ziyâsının işrak ve inbisâtıyla bakanlara iyân olmasıdır

rows.speaker: müfessirîn
rows.claim: Because the word is attached to the sun, exegetes interpret its duha as the sun’s radiance as it shines.
rows.anchor: müfessirîn bunu Güneş’in işrak ile parlayan ziyâsı diye tefsir etmişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath first invokes the sun in all its properties and then especially its light when it appears.
rows.anchor: Evvelâ Güneş’in zâhir olsun olmasın bütün hususiyetleriyle ale’l-ıtlâk kendisine, sonra da bilhassa zuhûru hâlindeki ziyâsına kasem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun drives major movements and transformations in the celestial system and life, both at rising and setting; its light makes the physical world visible and reveals its Creator’s care and power.
rows.anchor: Güneş tulû‘unda da gurûbunda da havâss-ı mahsûsasıyla manzûmesindeki hareket ve hayat tehavvülâtının başlıca bir menşe’ ve medârı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heat and light are its clearest benefits; both are felt especially at duha, and the sun’s heat connects to the preceding surah’s fire while light is what first strikes the eye.
rows.anchor: Güneş pek âteşîn bir menba‘-ı harâret olmak itibariyle evvelki sûrenin âhirindeki nâr ile münasebetdardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Light presents external forms to conscious sight; through reflection between the world and the self, together with other senses, it develops spiritual understanding and guides recognition of God.
rows.anchor: ziyânın böyle âfâk ile enfüs arasında peyderpey akislerle şuura iktirânından husûle gelen bu ta‘ayyünâttan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This illumination can lead purified souls to return contentedly to God and attain success under the call to enter among His servants and Paradise.
rows.anchor: رَاضِيَةًۭ مَّرْضِيَّةًۭ Rabbine rücû‘eder de فَٱدْخُلِى فِى عِبَٰدِى وَٱدْخُلِى جَنَّتِى hitâbıyla

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Light becomes fully meaningful in conscious perception, joining external and internal experience; it models how awareness links people to what lies beyond them, while creatures without consciousness have no concept of sun or light.
rows.anchor: gözü ve şuuru olmayanlar için nûr ve ziyâ ve Güneş mefhûmu yoktur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording draws attention to the sun’s illuminating and guiding role, then moves through changing light and darkness, the heavens and earth, and the soul’s inspired good and evil toward purification and success.
rows.anchor: ma‘kūlât ve ma‘neviyyât ile seyr-i enfüsîde tezekkî ve terakki ve felâha sevk ü irşad için şu kasemler
